title: How Andy Warhol Worked
summary: Hosts profile Andy Warhol's life and career: his Pittsburgh childhood and illness, commercial illustration in New York, the origins of pop art (Campbell's soup cans, silk-screen celebrity portraits, the Marilyn series), the Factory and his assistants and "superstars" such as Edie Sedgwick, filmmaking (Sleep, Empire, The Chelsea Girls), the 1968 shooting by Valerie Solanas, his later "business art" and 1980s MTV work, his Time Capsules, IRS audits, diaries, and death in 1987. Also covers the "fifteen minutes of fame" quote attribution and a listener mail segment about the Hammond organ and pianist Patricia Prattis Jennings.

segments.title: Intro and the fifteen minutes of fame quote
segments.summary: Hosts introduce Warhol and note he did not originate the 'fifteen minutes of fame' line, and that he treated himself as his own work of art.

segments.title: Childhood in Pittsburgh and early commercial career
segments.summary: Warhol's Pittsburgh childhood, his supportive family, illness (Sydenham chorea) and time in bed drawing, his father's death when he was 14, and his move to New York in 1949 where he became a successful commercial illustrator with a blotted-ink drawing style.

segments.title: Commercial art versus gallery art
segments.summary: Warhol did not see gallery art as more elevated than commercial work and let gallery owners and buyers shape his work.

segments.title: Early gallery work, sexuality, and his mother
segments.summary: Early self-published books and first solo show, his openness about gay themes in the 1950s, and his mother living with him until about 1971 when she died; his religious background and disputed stories.

segments.title: Warhol's contradictions and reputation
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Warhol as kind and giving but also cruel, and as a known liar whose quotes are often unreliable.

segments.title: Origins of pop art and the abstract expressionist backlash
segments.summary: Pop art's origins in London and Dada-influenced mass-produced imagery; contrast with Jackson Pollock and abstract expressionism; de Kooning's criticism; early celebrity silk screens such as Marilyn on gold.

segments.title: Campbell's soup cans, tracing, and silk screening
segments.summary: Warhol's early pop works including Coca-Cola bottles and the 1962 Campbell's soup can portraits, which he traced from projections; the idea was paid for at fifty dollars from Muriel Latow; switch to silk screen allowed repeated tomato soup can variants.

segments.title: Fairest Gallery show, mockery, and the Blum purchase
segments.summary: The 1962 Ferus Gallery solo show in Los Angeles with soup cans on shelves, critics mocking the work, Dennis Hopper's purchase, and Irving Blum buying back the thirty-two portraits for about a thousand dollars; a later soup can sold for $11.8 million in 2006.

segments.title: Paper dresses and interpreting the soup cans
segments.summary: Paper dresses with silk-screened images and a sale price near twelve million dollars; hosts discuss how the repeated brand image dissolves into color.

segments.title: Consumerism, ambition, and business art
segments.summary: Pop art as a comment or simple celebration of everyday things; Warhol as a consumer and sellout from the beginning, including a fake ad in The Village Voice; critics say his good period ran from 1961 to 1964.

segments.title: Influencer idea and the filmmaking
segments.summary: Warhol as an early self-promoter; his films such as Sleep, Empire, and The Chelsea Girls, which had no plots and were shown in avant-garde venues.

segments.title: The Factory, assistants, and ghost artists
segments.summary: The Silver Factory on East 47th Street in 1964, its name and history; assistant Gerard Malanga; the assembly-line production of works Warhol signed; comparison with ghost artists in the wider art world.

segments.title: Factory scene, Velvet Underground, and drugs
segments.summary: Description of the Factory crowd, Velvet Underground management and the banana album cover with Nico, and the wild, permissive atmosphere.

segments.title: Warhol's superstars and vampire reputation
segments.summary: Warhol collecting talent and misfits; Bob Colicello as human tape recorder; Bridget Berlin's work; Fran Lebowitz's vampire comment; Edie Sedgwick's relationship with Warhol and her 1971 death from overdose at 28.

segments.title: Other superstars: Candy Darling, Jackie Curtis, Ondine, Joe Dallesandro
segments.summary: Candy Darling and Jackie Curtis; Ondine's first meeting with Warhol; Joe Dallesandro as a film actor and the Sticky Fingers cover.

segments.title: Valerie Solanas and the 1968 shooting
segments.summary: I Shot Andy Warhol film with Lili Taylor; Solanas as the author of the SCUM Manifesto and her play Up Your Ass; the lost manuscript; June 3, 1968 shooting at the Union Square Factory; Warhol's injuries and corset.

segments.title: Later career, high society, and 1980s work
segments.summary: After the shooting Warhol moved toward high society and business art portraits; Ondine's career was dragged down; 1980s MTV shows, collaborations with Basquiat and Haring, and the late Last Supper series.

segments.title: Time Capsules, IRS audits, diaries, and death
segments.summary: Time Capsules project of 1974 onward; IRS audits from 1972 possibly linked to Nixon after McGovern campaign art; diaries dictated by phone; death in February 1987 at 58 after gallbladder surgery complications; the Andy Warhol Foundation and Pittsburgh museum.

segments.title: Andy Hunts diner idea and cringe interviews
segments.summary: Warhol's idea for Andy Mat diners with individual TV sets, and his cringey interviews including the Mike Douglas show with Edie Sedgwick.

segments.title: Wrap-up
segments.summary: Hosts conclude the Warhol overview and transition to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail on Hammond organs and Patricia Prattis Jennings
segments.summary: A retired Pittsburgh Symphony pianist writes about the Hammond organ episode and about Patricia Prattis Jennings, a pianist and early Black woman with a major symphony contract.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank the listener and give the email address for listener mail; standard show sign-off.
